theme: 宠物-工作犬野外走失事件

content.text: Shiyan, Lightning has been found! It's lying next to my backpack, looking exhausted but safe and sound. I'll send you a photo.
Great! I've seen the photo, and it looks like it's in good condition. You sound a bit choked up, so take a moment to calm down. How did you find it?
Well, thanks to your previous advice. I climbed to the highest point, repeatedly scanned with a telephoto lens, and finally spotted the reflection of the collar in a wind-sheltered rock crevice.
Good observation skills, you've persevered. How was the rock crevice environment? What was Lightning's condition at the time?
I took a photo of it while it was hiding. Look, it's curled up inside, appearing very alert, probably both cold and scared.

Well, this is typical behavior of a small dog after getting lost in an open area: initial excitement and chasing, followed by panic and hiding. Lightning might have gotten tired from chasing and instinctively sought a place to take shelter.
You're right, it's usually very lively in the wild, but this time it was probably scared. When I found it, it was still trembling a bit, so I quickly held it in my arms.

Safety first, glad you found your way. You handled this situation much more calmly than the last time you got lost. I remember you shared how to deal with thunderstorms in Session 4, and you’ve made great progress.
Thank you, it's all thanks to your guidance. This is a photo of me holding it after I found it; it's much calmer now.
I've seen the photos, and it looks like you're recovering well. Let's review: What was the root cause of Lightning's disappearance? Did you mention earlier that it was chasing something?

At that moment, I was photographing wildflowers in the meadow when Lightning suddenly dashed off to chase a rabbit, and I didn't manage to hold onto the leash in time. With the open view on the plateau, he got excited and ran far away.

This reminds us that even when the environment appears safe, we must not let our guard down. As discussed in Session 3 regarding emergency plans, unexpected situations are common in the wilderness, and teamwork, including pet management, is essential.

Yes, I was too focused on filming and neglected the dynamics of the lightning. In the future, I need to increase the safety margin as you emphasized, such as using a longer leash or training for recall.
Being pragmatic is good. Additionally, the reflective collar on Lightning was a great help, which aligns with your Session 2 approach to optimizing gear—key items should stand out.
Yes, the collar is made of reflective material. I didn't expect it to come in handy here. Shi Yan, how is your knee doing? Has there been any progress in long-term management since Session 7?

Much better, the daily soreness has lessened, but it still hurts when descending steep slopes. However, I’ve been practicing swimming as you suggested. This incident also made me realize that both the safety of field workers themselves and their companions should be taken seriously.

Well, from Session 1 until now, we've been learning to revere nature. After retrieving the lightning, I've come to understand the meaning of teamwork even more—not just among people, but including these little ones as well.
Well summarized. The incident has come to an end, but reflection must continue. What are your plans next? Will you continue filming?
First, let Lightning rest for a few days, and then we might try some light hiking, like the rehabilitative hikes in Session 6, balancing filming and its training.
Steady and sure. Let me know if you need route suggestions anytime—safety first. Lightning is fine now, so you can relax a bit. You handled this very methodically.
